info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 3.3: AI-Assisted Imaging in Historical Document Studies.

name.text: 01 Question: The AI Paradigm Shift: From Deterministic Filters to Statistical Vision Models

questiontext.text: What is the essential difference between `-deskew` and an AI vision model?

generalfeedback.text: Deterministic tools measure pixels; AI vision models recognize meaning by pattern, which makes their output a proposal rather than a measurement.

answer.text: `-deskew` reports a measurement, while the model reports a recognition that may be confidently wrong.

feedback.text: Correct. That is why AI output is a proposal to be judged rather than a result to be trusted.

answer.text: `-deskew` is slower but more thorough, since it examines every pixel individually.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed is not the distinction; the kind of claim each makes is.

answer.text: The AI model works on pixels while `-deskew` works on the meaning of the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is the other way round: deterministic tools work on pixels, models on patterns that carry meaning.

answer.text: They are equivalent, since both are software applied to the same image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One measures and one predicts, and the difference governs how much you check.

name.text: 02 Question: Overcoming the Manual Bottleneck: Why AI in Archival Imaging?

questiontext.text: Which part of facsimile work is AI actually aimed at?

generalfeedback.text: AI targets the repetitive part of facsimile work — tracing and typing coordinates — so editors can spend time on interpretation instead.

answer.text: The repetitive tracing of regions and typing of coordinates, which scales badly as pages multiply.

feedback.text: Correct. The intention is to free editorial time for interpretation, not to replace it.

answer.text: Deciding which features of a document are worth marking.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That judgement stays with the editor throughout this lesson.

answer.text: Determining the rights and licence conditions attached to an image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rights are a legal and curatorial question, not a vision task.

answer.text: Choosing which manuscript a scholar should edit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a research decision, not a processing bottleneck.

name.text: 03 Question: Computer Vision Foundations: Convolutional Networks, Vision Transformers, and Multimodal LLMs

questiontext.text: How do the three model families differ in practical use?

generalfeedback.text: CNNs and vision transformers are specialists for finding regions; multimodal language models are generalists you instruct in ordinary language.

answer.text: CNNs and vision transformers are specialists you run over many pages; multimodal language models are generalists you instruct in ordinary language.

feedback.text: Correct. Knowing which kind of tool you are holding tells you how to give it work.

answer.text: CNNs handle text, vision transformers handle images, and multimodal models handle audio.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CNNs and ViTs are both vision architectures; multimodal models combine image and text.

answer.text: Only multimodal models can produce coordinates; the others produce prose descriptions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Segmentation models exist precisely to produce regions and coordinates.

answer.text: They are three names for the same architecture used by different vendors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. They are genuinely different designs with different strengths.

name.text: 04 Question: Machine-Readable Layout Analysis: Document Image Analysis (DIA)

questiontext.text: A Dickinson poem's line runs onto a second line because the paper ran out. How do physical and logical layout differ here?

generalfeedback.text: Layout analysis separates where marks sit from what they mean, and the gap between the two is exactly where editorial judgement is required.

answer.text: Physically there are two lines, logically one, and the gap between them is where editorial judgement is required.

feedback.text: Correct. The machine sees the paper; you know the poem.

answer.text: Physically one line, logically two, because the poem counts each visual row separately.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The wrap is caused by the sheet, not by the poem's structure.

answer.text: They are identical, since layout analysis records exactly what is on the page.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Recording position and interpreting meaning are different operations.

answer.text: The distinction applies only to printed documents, not to manuscripts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manuscripts are where it matters most, since the writing surface constrains the hand.

name.text: 05 Question: Automated Page Segmentation: Distinguishing Margins, Headers, and Text Blocks

questiontext.text: What should you expect to find when you check a segmentation model's output on a stained document?

generalfeedback.text: Segmentation returns labelled regions with coordinates, giving you a draft set of zones — including plausible-looking zones around stains.

answer.text: Plausible-looking zones drawn around stains, alongside the genuine regions.

feedback.text: Correct. Segmentation gives you a draft set of zones, and drafts contain errors that look convincing.

answer.text: Stains are ignored automatically, since they contain no ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models routinely mark discoloured areas as text blocks.

answer.text: The model refuses to process pages with significant damage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It will process them and return confident output.

answer.text: Stains are flagged separately as damage with a warning label.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Only a model trained for damage detection would do that, and it is not the default.

name.text: 06 Question: Baseline Detection and Text-Line Segmentation: Kraken, dhSegment, and Transkribus

questiontext.text: Why do modern tools trace baselines rather than drawing a rectangle around each line?

generalfeedback.text: Baselines follow the wander of real handwriting, separating interlocking lines that rectangles cannot.

answer.text: In real handwriting, descenders and ascenders from neighbouring lines fall inside any rectangle drawn around a line.

feedback.text: Correct. A traced baseline and its contour separate lines that overlap.

answer.text: Rectangles cannot be stored in TEI, whereas baselines can.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI stores rectangles readily; the problem is that they capture the wrong pixels.

answer.text: Baselines are faster to compute than rectangles.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Accuracy on interlocking hands, not speed, is the reason.

answer.text: Rectangles distort when the image is deskewed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deskewing affects all coordinates equally; overlap is the issue here.

name.text: 07 Question: Generating TEI `<zone>` Coordinates with AI: From Polygons to Bounding Boxes

questiontext.text: A zone in your file appears offset from the feature it should mark. What is the most likely cause?

generalfeedback.text: AI output must be converted from x/y/width/height into TEI's corner attributes, and most coordinate errors happen in that conversion rather than in the model.

answer.text: A conversion error between the model's x, y, width, height output and TEI's corner attributes.

feedback.text: Correct. Most coordinate errors enter at the conversion step rather than in the model's prediction.

answer.text: The model was trained on documents in a different language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language does not shift coordinates systematically.

answer.text: The TEI schema rejected the coordinates and substituted defaults.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A schema validates; it never rewrites your values.

answer.text: The image was saved as PNG rather than JPEG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. File format does not change pixel positions.

name.text: 08 Question: Addressing Complex Layouts: Multi-Column Broadsides and Interlinear Additions

questiontext.text: Why should reading order be checked before the coordinates on a two-column printed decree?

generalfeedback.text: Columns and interlinear variants break automatic reading order, so verify sequence before you trust any zone-to-text links.

answer.text: A model reading straight down the page will alternate between columns, so perfectly placed zones can be attached to the wrong lines.

feedback.text: Correct. A well-placed zone linked to the wrong text is worse than no zone at all.

answer.text: Reading order determines the resolution at which zones are calculated.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution and sequence are unrelated.

answer.text: Coordinates cannot be computed until reading order is fixed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Coordinates are computed independently; the risk is in the linking.

answer.text: Columns make the page too wide for automatic segmentation to run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Segmentation runs; it is the sequencing that fails.

name.text: 09 Question: Vernacular and Irregular Handwriting: Overcoming Folk Script Challenges

questiontext.text: A model loses the baseline halfway across a page of Maud Lewis's handwriting. What does that indicate?

generalfeedback.text: Models fail on irregular everyday hands because their training data was tidier than the document, not because the document is deficient.

answer.text: A mismatch between the document and the tidier material the model was trained on, not a defect in the handwriting.

feedback.text: Correct. The remedies are a model trained on handwriting, or fine-tuning on corrected pages of your own.

answer.text: That the image resolution is too low for any model to process.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Resolution may matter, but drifting baselines on unruled paper are the described cause.

answer.text: That the handwriting is too irregular to be transcribed by anyone.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A human reader manages; the limitation is the model's training.

answer.text: That the page must be binarized before segmentation will work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Binarization may help slightly but does not address training mismatch.

name.text: 10 Question: Non-Textual Feature Detection: Identifying Seals, Signatures, and Totemic Marks

questiontext.text: How should the signatory marks on a treaty be handled in your encoding?

generalfeedback.text: Seals, signatures, and signatory marks should be encoded as typed zones rather than forced into text, and naming their type is an editorial judgement.

answer.text: As typed zones recording where they are and what they are, rather than being forced into text.

feedback.text: Correct. Choosing the type is an editorial judgement about what the document is.

answer.text: As transcribed characters, using the closest available letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Forcing marks into letters misrepresents what is on the page.

answer.text: As image noise to be removed before processing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These marks carry the document's legal force.

answer.text: As metadata in the header only, with no position recorded.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Their position on the page is part of the evidence.

name.text: 11 Question: Automated Image Organization: Clustering, Duplicate Detection, and Sorting

questiontext.text: Clustering has grouped two near-identical captures of the same page. What remains your decision?

generalfeedback.text: Clustering can group duplicates and flag gaps in a capture sequence, but which duplicate survives is an editorial decision.

answer.text: Which of the two to keep, since the software groups by appearance and cannot know which one you want.

feedback.text: Correct. Safer practice is to move rejects aside rather than delete them.

answer.text: Whether the two images are duplicates at all, since clustering cannot detect similarity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Detecting similarity is exactly what clustering does well.

answer.text: Which file format each should be converted to before grouping.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Format conversion is unrelated to the grouping decision.

answer.text: Nothing: the tool deletes the weaker capture automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Automatic deletion of evidence is precisely what you should avoid.

name.text: 12 Question: Smart Image Naming: Deriving Standardized File Names from Document Content

questiontext.text: Why is an incorrect automated filename more dangerous than a meaningless one?

generalfeedback.text: Automated renaming saves hours but writes its mistakes into every later citation, so verify a sample before renaming in bulk.

answer.text: A plausible but wrong name propagates into the TEI, the citations, and the published edition, and nothing downstream questions it.

feedback.text: Correct. Spot-check a sample before letting a script rename a whole directory.

answer.text: Incorrect names break the file system and make the images unreadable.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The files still open; the error is bibliographic, not technical.

answer.text: Meaningless names cannot be corrected later, whereas wrong ones can.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both can be corrected; the wrong one is unlikely to be noticed.

answer.text: Wrong names cause validation errors in the TEI schema.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A schema cannot know whether a filename describes the right side of a leaf.

name.text: 13 Question: Metadata Extraction at Scale: Reading Dates, Archival Stamps, and Catalog Numbers

questiontext.text: A model extracts an accession number from a faint archival stamp. What should you do with it?

generalfeedback.text: AI is good at finding marginal stamps and shelfmarks and unreliable at reading them exactly, so verify every extracted identifier against the catalogue.

answer.text: Read it yourself from the image and check it against the institution's catalogue before writing it into the header.

feedback.text: Correct. A number wrong in one digit looks exactly like a correct one, and no schema will object.

answer.text: Record it with `@cert="low"` and publish it without further checking.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Marking uncertainty is good practice but does not replace verification that is available.

answer.text: Accept it, since extraction models are trained specifically on archival stamps.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Finding the stamp is reliable; reading it exactly is not.

answer.text: Discard it, since identifiers should never be taken from images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The image is a legitimate source; it simply requires verification.

name.text: 14 Question: Automated Quality Control: Detecting Blur, Glare, Incomplete Scans, and Cropping Errors

questiontext.text: What makes automated quality control valuable even for a single page?

generalfeedback.text: Automated checks for focus, glare, edges, and reference targets catch failures while the object is still accessible.

answer.text: It applies the checks — focus, glare, edges, reference target — while the object is still in front of you.

feedback.text: Correct. The alternative is discovering the problem after the archive has closed the file.

answer.text: It repairs defocused and glared images automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It detects problems; it cannot fix a capture that failed.

answer.text: It replaces the need for a scale bar and colour target.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One of its checks is that those references are present.

answer.text: It certifies images as meeting national digitization standards.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a checklist, not a certification.

name.text: 15 Question: AI-Assisted Super-Resolution and Denoising: Opportunities and Hallucination Risks

questiontext.text: Why is super-resolution unacceptable as a basis for transcription?

generalfeedback.text: Super-resolution invents detail rather than recovering it, so it must never inform transcription and must be disclosed wherever it is shown.

answer.text: It generates detail that was never captured, so an ambiguous mark can be rendered as a definite accent or comma that never existed.

feedback.text: Correct. A blurry image is more honest, because it shows its own uncertainty.

answer.text: It reduces the image's resolution as a side effect of enlargement.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It increases apparent resolution; the problem is that the added detail is invented.

answer.text: It is too slow to apply to a whole manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed is not the objection; fabricated evidence is.

answer.text: It cannot be applied to greyscale images.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It applies to any image, which is part of the danger.

name.text: 16 Question: Automated Contrast and Ink Recovery: Deep Learning for Faded and Stained Inks

questiontext.text: How does model-based ink recovery differ from the contrast stretching you used on Wednesday?

generalfeedback.text: Model-based ink recovery may see through stains that arithmetic cannot, but it belongs in a separate, labelled layer beside the untouched original.

answer.text: Contrast stretching redistributes recorded brightness, while the model produces an image mixing recorded and inferred detail that cannot afterwards be separated.

feedback.text: Correct. That is why it belongs in a labelled layer beside the untouched original.

answer.text: There is no difference; both adjust brightness values mathematically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One is arithmetic on what was recorded; the other adds inference.

answer.text: Model-based recovery is deterministic, so it needs no disclosure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Trained models are not deterministic in the sense Lesson 3.2 used.

answer.text: Contrast stretching invents detail, while model recovery only amplifies it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. This reverses the two.

name.text: 17 Question: Verso Show-Through and Bleed-Through Removal via Neural Image Separation

questiontext.text: You have photographs of both sides of a leaf. Which method should you prefer for removing show-through, and why?

generalfeedback.text: Use the two-sided deterministic method where you can, because removing ghosts from a single image is inference, and ghosts are themselves evidence.

answer.text: The deterministic two-sided method, because it proves where the ghost came from instead of inferring it.

feedback.text: Correct. And remember that visible show-through is itself evidence about the paper and the ink.

answer.text: The model-based method, because it produces a cleaner result with less work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A cleaner result built on inference is a weaker claim.

answer.text: Either, since both produce identical output from the same inputs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. One subtracts measured evidence; the other predicts what to remove.

answer.text: Neither: show-through can only be removed by rephotographing under raking light.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Raking light addresses surface topography, not ink showing through.

name.text: 18 Question: Aligning Images with Transcriptions: The Text-Image Alignment Problem

questiontext.text: Why is forced alignment the most trustworthy AI method in this lesson?

generalfeedback.text: Forced alignment is reliable precisely because the transcription is supplied: the model locates known words instead of guessing unknown ones.

answer.text: The correct transcription is supplied in advance, so the model only has to locate known words rather than guess what they say.

feedback.text: Correct. The machine answers a question it is good at, and you keep the one you are good at.

answer.text: It is deterministic, producing identical coordinates on every run.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is still a model; its reliability comes from the constraint on the task.

answer.text: It only works on printed documents, where the text is unambiguous.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is used on handwriting as well.

answer.text: It verifies the transcription against the image and corrects errors in it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It assumes the transcription is authoritative; it does not audit it.

name.text: 19 Question: Automated Insertion of `<facsimile>`, `<surface>`, and `<graphic>` in TEI XML

questiontext.text: In a scripted facsimile pipeline, which part is a prediction rather than a measurement?

generalfeedback.text: Assembling the facsimile block is scripted and deterministic; only the zone coordinates are predictions, and that is where checking belongs.

answer.text: The zone coordinates proposed by the model; dimensions are measured and the XML is assembled by rule.

feedback.text: Correct. Knowing which parts are certain tells you where checking belongs.

answer.text: The image dimensions, since the script estimates them from the file type.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dimensions are read directly from the file.

answer.text: The placement of the `` block, which the script infers from the document structure.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Its position is fixed by the TEI Guidelines.

answer.text: The `xml:id` values, which the model invents for each surface.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Identifiers are generated by a predictable rule in the script.

name.text: 20 Question: Linking Text Elements to Image Zones: Automating `@facs` and `@corresp`

questiontext.text: A file full of `@facs` pointers validates cleanly but nothing highlights in the viewer. What has gone wrong?

generalfeedback.text: Scripts can insert every `@facs` pointer at once, but only clicking through the result proves the pointers land where they should.

answer.text: The pointers refer to identifiers that do not exist, which a schema does not check.

feedback.text: Correct. Only clicking through the result proves the pointers land where they should.

answer.text: The `@facs` values are missing their `#`, which would have failed validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A missing `#` is possible, but the schema would still not catch a dangling target.

answer.text: The zones were defined after the text, so they load too late.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Order of elements does not affect whether a pointer resolves.

answer.text: The viewer requires `@corresp` rather than `@facs`.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `@facs` is the standard attribute for this link.

name.text: 21 Question: Multi-Witness Alignment: Cross-Referencing Manuscript Variants

questiontext.text: Alignment software reports that two Dickinson copies differ at a particular word. What has it told you?

generalfeedback.text: Alignment tools find where witnesses differ; deciding what a difference means remains the editor's work.

answer.text: Where the witnesses differ, but not whether the difference is a revision, a correction, or a copying slip.

feedback.text: Correct. Alignment is a finding aid; interpreting the variant is editorial work.

answer.text: Which reading is authorial and should be adopted in the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. No alignment tool can establish authorial intention.

answer.text: That one of the two transcriptions contains an error.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A genuine variant is not a transcription error.

answer.text: The chronological order in which the two copies were written.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Dating is inferred from other evidence.

name.text: 22 Question: IIIF Annotation Generation: Producing Web Annotation Data Model JSON-LD with AI

questiontext.text: How does a IIIF annotation relate to a TEI zone?

generalfeedback.text: IIIF annotations express the same coordinates as TEI zones in a form any viewer can read, so one pipeline can publish both.

answer.text: It expresses the same coordinates in a different notation, so one pipeline can publish both.

feedback.text: Correct. The advantage of the IIIF form is that any compliant viewer can read it.

answer.text: It replaces the TEI zone, since the two cannot coexist in one project.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editions routinely publish both.

answer.text: It records the licence conditions of the region rather than its position.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An annotation links content to a region.

answer.text: It stores the image data itself, whereas a zone only points at coordinates.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Annotations point at regions; they do not carry pixels.

name.text: 23 Question: Fine-Tuning Vision Models on Historical Hands and Document Types

questiontext.text: What does fine-tuning require, and what does that imply about manual work?

generalfeedback.text: Fine-tuning adapts a general model using a few pages you corrected yourself, so manual accuracy is the foundation of machine accuracy.

answer.text: A small set of pages you have corrected yourself, which means machine accuracy is built on manual accuracy.

feedback.text: Correct. Ten to twenty carefully checked pages is a realistic amount.

answer.text: Thousands of unlabelled images of similar documents.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fine-tuning starts from a pre-trained model and needs only a small curated sample.

answer.text: A commercial licence for the underlying model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Many models suitable for fine-tuning are openly available.

answer.text: That all manual encoding be finished before the model can be used at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A small ground-truth sample is enough to begin.

name.text: 24 Question: Active Learning and Human-in-the-Loop: Correcting AI Predictions Iteratively

questiontext.text: In a human-in-the-loop workflow, which output should you review first?

generalfeedback.text: Review the model's least confident output first, feed corrections back, and keep the record of what it got wrong.

answer.text: The predictions the model is least confident about, with your corrections fed back for the next batch.

feedback.text: Correct. It also produces a record of what the machine got wrong and how often.

answer.text: The first pages processed, since early errors propagate through the batch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Each page is processed independently; confidence is the better ordering.

answer.text: A random sample, to avoid biasing your attention.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sampling is useful for audit, but triage by confidence uses your time better.

answer.text: The highest-confidence predictions, to confirm the model is working.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those need the least attention.

name.text: 25 Question: Confidence Scoring and Error Detection: When Does the Vision Model Fail?

questiontext.text: Which failure is described as the dangerous one, and why?

generalfeedback.text: Confidence scores triage review but do not guarantee correctness; record uncertainty in the markup with `@cert` rather than hiding it.

answer.text: A missed faint marginal note, because an absent zone looks like nothing at all rather than like an error.

feedback.text: Correct. Errors that leave no trace are the ones review procedures must be designed to catch.

answer.text: A zone drawn around a stain, because it adds false content to the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It is a real error, but a visible one you will notice on review.

answer.text: A baseline that drifts on a warped leaf, because it cannot be corrected by hand.

feedback.text: Incorrect. It can be corrected, and it is visible.

answer.text: A low confidence score, because it prevents the zone from being written at all.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Low confidence is information, not a failure.

name.text: 26 Question: Ethical and Scholarly Integrity: The Risk of Generative Hallucination in Archival Images

questiontext.text: Why is silently altering a facsimile image the most serious form of misrepresentation in an edition?

generalfeedback.text: Never generate missing content in a facsimile; enhancements are labelled derivatives and the method belongs in the header.

answer.text: A reader can check a transcription against the image, but cannot check the image against an object they will never see.

feedback.text: Correct. The image is where the reader's trust terminates, so it must not be quietly changed.

answer.text: Because image files are harder to correct than XML files once published.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Technical difficulty is not the issue; verifiability is.

answer.text: Because copyright in the image usually belongs to the holding institution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Rights matter, but the point here is evidential integrity.

answer.text: Because generative tools leave detectable artefacts that discredit the edition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The wrong is done whether or not it is detected.

name.text: 27 Question: The Black Box Problem: Explainability and Reproducibility in AI Imaging Workflows

questiontext.text: What should you preserve so that AI-assisted work survives the tool that produced it?

generalfeedback.text: AI results are not reliably reproducible, so record versions and settings and keep the checked output rather than depending on a service.

answer.text: The checked output itself, together with the model version and settings you used.

feedback.text: Correct. Publish what you verified rather than a dependency on a service that may be withdrawn.

answer.text: A link to the commercial service, so readers can rerun the analysis themselves.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Services are updated and retired, and results change without notice.

answer.text: Only the final TEI file, since it contains everything a reader needs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Without versions and settings, the method cannot be assessed.

answer.text: The training data the model was built from.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is rarely available and is not what makes your result checkable.

name.text: 28 Question: Integrating AI Pipelines with Open-Source Deterministic Tools

questiontext.text: Where does the AI step sit in a production imaging pipeline?

generalfeedback.text: In production, deterministic processing brackets the AI step on both sides, and its proposals enter the edition only after review.

answer.text: In the middle: deterministic processing prepares the images, the model proposes regions, and deterministic tools then cut derivatives and tiles.

feedback.text: Correct. The proposals enter the edition only after you accept them.

answer.text: First, so that its output determines how the images should be processed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models perform better on clean, consistent input.

answer.text: Last, as a final check on the deterministic output.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The final steps are deterministic derivative generation and human review.

answer.text: Alongside, running independently of the deterministic tools.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The steps are sequential and each depends on the previous one.

name.text: 29 Question: Building an End-to-End AI Imaging Pipeline: From Raw Scans to Validated TEI/IIIF

questiontext.text: In the eight-step pipeline, which steps are AI proposals?

generalfeedback.text: In the full pipeline only layout analysis and alignment are AI proposals; the rest is measured, scripted, or editorial.

answer.text: Layout analysis and alignment; the rest is measured, scripted, or editorial.

feedback.text: Correct. Knowing which is which is what the module was teaching.

answer.text: Normalization and derivative generation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both are deterministic operations with recorded parameters.

answer.text: Capture checking and final review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are your judgement, assisted at most by a checklist.

answer.text: Every step after capture.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Most of the pipeline is deterministic or editorial.

name.text: 30 Question: The Methodological Triad: Synthesizing Manual, Deterministic, and AI-Assisted Imaging

questiontext.text: Why does the course insist on the order manual, then deterministic, then AI?

generalfeedback.text: Manual work sets the standard, deterministic tools scale it, and AI proposes at speed — which is only safe in that order.

answer.text: Manual work establishes what correct looks like, deterministic tools scale it, and only then can you recognize when the machine is wrong.

feedback.text: Correct. The same order returns in Module 4, where a confident machine error becomes words in your edition.

answer.text: Because the manual and deterministic tools are older and must be taught first historically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The order is pedagogical and evidential, not chronological.

answer.text: Because AI tools are too expensive to use before the others have been tried.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cost is not the reason for the sequence.

answer.text: Because TEI requires manual encoding before any automation is permitted.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI imposes no such requirement; this is a scholarly method.
